title: The model that fit everything and predicted nothing
intro: A thermal model of an enclosure solves cleanly and matches the measured cooling curve. Asked to predict tomorrow's warm-up from a cold start, it produces a different answer every time it is run. Open the clues.

facts.label: The symptom
facts.value: Re-running the prediction gives a family of curves, all the same shape, stacked at different heights. Nobody can say which one the enclosure will follow.

facts.label: The equation
facts.value: First-order and separable: dT/dt = -k(T - T_ambient). Newton's law of cooling, correct for this enclosure.

facts.label: The fit
facts.value: Against the recorded cooling run the model matches to within sensor noise. k was identified from that data and is trusted.

facts.label: The solution as stored
facts.value: T(t) = T_ambient + C·e^(-kt). The constant C is left symbolic in the model definition.

facts.label: The prediction call
facts.value: The warm-up prediction supplies t, k and T_ambient. It does not supply a starting temperature — there is no argument for one.

facts.label: The order
facts.value: The equation is first order, so its general solution carries exactly one arbitrary constant.

composition.label: General solution used where a particular one was needed

question: What actually failed?
choices: k was identified from cooling data and does not transfer to warming
The model is only a general solution — a one-parameter family — and nothing supplies the initial condition that would select a single member
The equation needs to be second order to capture warm-up
Sensor noise in the original fit propagated into the prediction
debrief:
Nothing is wrong with the physics, the fit, or k. The model is a **general solution** — `T = T_ambient + C·e^(-kt)` — and a first-order equation's general solution carries exactly one arbitrary constant. That constant is a whole family of parallel behaviours, identical in shape, differing only in where they start.

The cooling run matched because the recorded data *implicitly* supplied the condition: the fit had a starting temperature to anchor to. The prediction has none, so C is unconstrained and every run is as valid as any other. The symptom in the first clue — same shape, different heights — is the visual signature of exactly this, and it is the same signature as the navigator's drift earlier in this pack. Both are a missing constant of integration wearing different clothes.

The fix is a measurement, not a better model: supply T(0). One number collapses the family to the single curve the enclosure will actually follow.

The broader habit is in the last clue. **Order tells you how many conditions you owe.** A first-order equation needs one; a second-order needs two, typically position and velocity. If you have fewer conditions than the order, you do not have a prediction — you have a family, and saying so is more useful than picking a member at random.
